claims.text: Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes, specifically plants and animals, is a documented phenomenon that plays a role in evolution, though it is less common than HGT among prokaryotes [Source: ev-1].
While this process is well-studied in bacteria where it facilitates antibiotic resistance and virulence [Source: ev-1], it also occurs in eukaryotic systems.

The table of contents for the Wikipedia article on HGT explicitly lists sections dedicated to Eukaryotes, including specific subsections for transfers such as Bacteria to plants (6.4), Plant to plant (6.6), Plants to animals (6.7), Animals to animals (6.14), and Human genome (6.17) [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: More recent instances often occur within intimate relationships, such as those between endosymbionts and their invertebrate hosts, particularly insects and nematodes, or in asexual animals [Source: ev-3].
These transfers are consistent with modern evolutionary theories like the serial endosymbiotic theory and Muller’s ratchet [Source: ev-3].
The evolutionary significance of HGT lies in its ability to allow organisms to acquire novel traits unique from those inherited vertically [Source: ev-3].

In prokaryotes, phylogenetic analysis of 144 genomes indicates that while most information flows vertically, genes are frequently transferred horizontally between closely related taxa or bacteria sharing the same environment [Source: ev-3].
Although less common than in eubacteria, HGT among eukaryotes has been identified and is considered an important factor in evolution [Source: ev-1][ev-3].

**Evolutionary Significance and Prevalence**
The evolutionary significance of HGT lies in its ability to allow organisms to acquire novel traits unique from those inherited vertically [Source: ev-3].
The rapid spread of such genes can challenge traditional views of the "tree of life," as indicated by section headings regarding challenges to this model [Source: ev-1].
